verses.zh: 他对我说：「人子啊，你站起来，我要和你说话。」
verses.en: He said to me, “Son of man,[NOTE:1] stand on your feet and I will speak with you.”
notes: The phrase son of man occurs ninety-three times in the book of Ezekiel. It simply means “human one” and distinguishes the prophet from the nonhuman beings that are present in the world of his vision.
verses.commentary:
2:1 "Son of man" This is literally "ben-Adam" (BDB 119 CONSTRUCT BDB 9). This is
used often in Ezekiel as a way of referring to Ezekiel as a human being (93 times, cf. Ps. 8:4). In Ezekiel it is the
way YHWH addresses Ezekiel. This same phrase is found in Ps. 8:4 in parallel with "man" (i.e. Enosh, BDB 60 and
Adam, BDB 9).

In Dan. 7:13 this term takes on divine characteristics as one likened to "a son of man" coming before
the Ancient of Days (i.e. Deity) riding on the clouds of heaven. Daniel 7:13 is the background for Jesus' use of this
term for himself, which combines humanity and deity (i.e. 1 John 4:1-3). The phrase had no nationalistic or militaristic
rabbinical overtones.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SON OF MAN

▣ YHWH addresses Ezekiel.

- "stand on your feet" (BDB 763, KB 840, Qal IMPERATIVE)

- "I may speak with you" (BDB 180, KB 210, Piel IMPERFECT, but
used in a COHORTATIVE sense [cf. Ezek. 2:2])

Notice the personal (cf. Ezek. 1:26) God of glory (cf. Ezek. 1:28) addresses Ezekiel! This is one of
the major themes of this book (the personal presence of YHWH in Babylon). Also note a mere human, a fallen human,
part of a rebellious people, is addressed face to face, standing before the holy presence. This says something of the
dignity of humanity made in the image and likeness of God (cf. Gen. 1:26-27).

verses.zh: 他对我说话的时候，灵就进入我里面，使我站起来，我便听见那位对我说话的声音。
verses.en: As he spoke to me,[NOTE:1] a wind[NOTE:2] came into me and stood me on my feet, and I heard the one speaking to me.
notes: The phrase “as he spoke to me” is absent from the LXX.

Or “spirit.” The NIV has “the Spirit,” but the absence of the article in the Hebrew text makes this unlikely. Elsewhere in Ezekiel the Lord’s Spirit is referred to as “the Spirit of the Lord” (11:5; 37:1), “the Spirit of God” (11:24), or “my (that is, the Lord’s) Spirit” (36:27; 37:14; 39:29). Some identify the “spirit” of 2:2 as the spirit that energized the living beings; however, that “spirit” is called “the spirit” (1:12, 20) or “the spirit of the living beings” (1:20-21; 10:17). Still others see the term as referring to an impersonal “spirit” of strength or courage, that is, the term may also be understood as a disposition or attitude. The Hebrew word often refers to a wind in Ezekiel (1:4; 5:10, 12; 12:4; 13:11, 13; 17:10, 21; 19:12; 27:26; 37:9). In 37:5-10 a “breath” originates in the “four winds” and is associated with the Lord’s life-giving breath (see v. 14). This breath enters into the dry bones and gives them life. In a similar fashion the breath of 2:2 (see also 3:24) energizes paralyzed Ezekiel. Breath and wind are related. On the one hand, it is a more normal picture to think of breath rather than wind entering someone, but since wind represents an external force, it seems more likely for wind rather than breath to stand someone up (unless we should understand it as a disposition). It may be that one should envision the breath of the speaker moving like a wind to revive Ezekiel, helping him to regain his breath and invigorating him to stand. A wind also transports the prophet from one place to another (3:12, 14; 8:3; 11:1, 24; 43:5).
verses.commentary:
2:2 "the Spirit entered me" It is not certain if we are speaking of the Holy Spirit or, more probably, simply
personal imagery parallel to "the hand of the Lord" from Ezek. 1:3 (cf. Ezek. 3:14; 33:22;
37:1; 40:1). A non-human life force (ruah, BDB 924) entered me (i.e. divine wind or breath, cf. Ezek. 37:9,14).
The term "spirit" has no ARTICLE in Hebrew (see SPECIAL TOPIC: BREATH, WIND, SPIRIT).

Ezekiel's call to the prophetic ministry is signaled in several characteristic phrases.

- "spirit/Spirit entered me" (cf. 1 Chr. 15:1; 20:14; 24:20; Isa. 61:1; Joel 2:28)

- "I am sending you" (cf. Ezek. 2:3, 4)

- "Thus says the Lord God"

- "do not fear them"

- "you shall speak My words to them"

- "eat the scroll," Ezek. 2:8-3:3

- "go to the house of Israel and speak with My words to them," Ezek. 3:4,11

- "spirit/Spirit lifted me up" (cf. Ezek. 8:3; 11:1,24)

For a good brief discussion of ruah (BDB 924) see Norman Siraith, The Distinctive Ideas of the
Old Testament, pp. 143-158.

verses.zh: 他对我说：「人子啊，我差你往悖逆的国民以色列人那里去。他们是悖逆我的，他们和他们的列祖违背我，直到今日。
verses.en: He said to me, “Son of man, I am sending you to the house[NOTE:1] of Israel, to rebellious nations[NOTE:2] who have rebelled against me; both they and their fathers have revolted[NOTE:3] against me to this very day.
notes: The Hebrew reads “sons of,” while the LXX reads “house,” implying the more common phrase in Ezekiel. Either could be abbreviated with the first letter ב (bet). In preparation for the characterization “house of rebellion,” in vv. 5, 6, and 8 “house” is preferred (L. C. Allen, Ezekiel [WBC], 1:10 and W. Zimmerli, Ezekiel [Hermeneia], 2:564-65).

Heb “to the rebellious nations.” The phrase “to the rebellious nations” is omitted in the LXX. Elsewhere in Ezekiel the singular word “nation” is used for Israel (36:13-15; 37:22). Here “nations” may have the meaning of “tribes” or refer to the two nations of Israel and Judah.

This word is omitted from the LXX. tn The Hebrew term used here is the strongest word available for expressing a covenant violation. The word is used in the diplomatic arena to express a treaty violation (2 Kgs 1:1; 3:5, 7).
verses.commentary:
2:3 "I am sending you to the sons of Israel, to a rebellious people" The phrase "sons of Israel" in the book of
Ezekiel is sometimes used for the Northern Ten Tribes, but most often it is used for all of the covenant people.

The term "rebellious" is a Qal PARTICIPLE (BDB 597, KB 632). It is
followed by a Qal PERFECT of the same VERB (lit.,
rebels who rebel). Their personal and continual rebellion is directed against the covenant God (i.e. "Me"). This is
what their fathers, grandfathers, and great grandfathers also did.

To this terrible characterization is added another
term for rebellion ("transgressed," BDB 833, KB 981, Qal PERFECT). This is defined as
"a rebellious nation" (cf. Exod. 32:9; 33:3,5; 34:9; Deut. 9:6,7,13; 10:16; 31:27; 2 Chr. 30:8; Acts 7:51).

The term "people" (BDB 156) is the term goim, which is often used contemptuously by the
Israelites of the pagan Gentile nations. It is PLURAL, which probably refers to Israel and Judah. The
Jewish Study Bible, p. 1048, says rabbinic commentators think it refers to Judah and Benjamin. This was purposeful sarcasm.

verses.zh: 这众子面无羞耻，心里刚硬。我差你往他们那里去，你要对他们说：主耶和华如此说。
verses.en: The people[NOTE:1] to whom I am sending you are obstinate and hard-hearted,[NOTE:2] and you must say to them, ‘This is what the Sovereign Lord says.’[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “sons.” The word choice may reflect treaty idiom, where the relationship between an overlord and his subjects can be described as that of father and son.
Heb “stern of face and hard of heart.” The phrases “stern of face” and “hard of heart” are lacking in the LXX.
The phrase “thus says [the Lord]” occurs 129 times in Ezekiel; the announcement is identical to the way messengers often introduced their messages (Gen 32:5; 45:9; Exod 5:10; Num 20:14; Judg 11:15).
verses.commentary:
2:4

NASB, TEV, NJB, REB
"stubborn"

NKJV, NRSV, Peshitta
"impudent"

JPSOA
"brazen of face"

This was originally an agricultural phrase referring to unruly oxen. Literally it means "hard of neck"
or "stiff-necked" (BDB 904, cf. Exod. 32:9; 33:3,5; 34:9; Deuteronomy 6; 7; 13; 24; 27; 10:16; 31:27).

SPECIAL TOPIC: STUBBORNNESS (OT)

NASB, NJB, REB
"obstinate"

NKJV, NRSV, JPSOA, Peshitta
"stubborn"

TEV
"do not respect me"

The second term (BDB 305 CONSTRUCT BDB 524, lit. "strong of heart"), in this
context, implies a hardness toward God and His revealed will (cf. Ezek. 3:7). What a striking series of descriptive
phrases characterizing the covenant people.

▣ "Lord God" This is "adonai - YHWH," which is a characteristic
title of God in the book of Ezekiel. It comes from the term Adon, which is the Hebrew term for "master-lord"
(BDB 10, KB 12) and the Covenant name for God, YHWH, from the Hebrew VERB "to be" (BDB 217, KB 394).

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD (adon and kurios)

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

verses.zh: 他们或听，或不听，（他们是悖逆之家），必知道在他们中间有了先知。
verses.en: And as for them,[NOTE:1] whether they listen[NOTE:2] or not—for they are a rebellious[NOTE:3] house[NOTE:4]—they will know that a prophet has been among them.
notes: Heb “they”; the phrase “And as for them” has been used in the translation for clarity.
The Hebrew word implies obedience rather than mere hearing or paying attention.
This Hebrew adjective is also used to describe the Israelites in Num 17:10 (17:25 HT) and Isa 30:9.
The book of Ezekiel frequently refers to the Israelites as a rebellious house (Ezek 2:5, 6, 8; 3:9, 26-27; 12:2-3, 9, 25; 17:12; 24:3).
verses.commentary:
2:5 "a rebellious house" This descriptive phrase (BDB 108 CONSTRUCT BDB 598) is used often in Ezekiel (cf. Ezek.
2:5,6,8; 3:9,26,27; 12:2 [twice],3,9,25; 17:12; 24:3; also note 44:6). Moses also saw this propensity in Israel (cf. Deut. 31:27, also
note Neh. 9:17), as did Samuel (cf. 1 Sam. 15:23) and Isaiah (cf. Isa. 30:9).

YHWH seems to have chosen a people who were notoriously stiff-necked and rebellious for the theological
purpose of demonstrating His long-suffering covenant faithfulness, even amidst their inability to faithful obedience! YHWH
did not choose the family of Abraham because of anything special in them, but to reveal His own character (i.e. Deut.
7:7,8; Isaiah 48; Jer. 7:24-26; 11:7-8). The OT is not primarily about Israel, but about YHWH!

SPECIAL TOPIC: STUBBORNNESS (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

▣ "whether they listen or not" This is a recurrent theme (cf. Ezek. 2:5,7; 3:11,27). This is parallel to
Isa. 6:9-10.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LISTEN/HEAR (shema)

▣ "they will know that a prophet has been among them" God chose to reveal His future actions in order that

- the people are responsible for their rebellious acts (cf. Ezek. 2:6-7; note Josh. 24:19-28)

- He is revealed as the only true God (i.e. predictive prophecy, cf. Jer. 28:9; Ezek. 33:33)

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE BIBLE (its uniqueness and inspiration)

verses.zh: 人子啊，虽有荆棘和蒺藜在你那里，你又住在蝎子中间，总不要怕他们，也不要怕他们的话；他们虽是悖逆之家，还不要怕他们的话，也不要因他们的脸色惊惶。
verses.en: But you, son of man, do not fear them, and do not fear their words. Even though briers[NOTE:1] and thorns[NOTE:2] surround you and you live among scorpions—do not fear their words and do not be terrified of the looks they give you,[NOTE:3] for they are a rebellious house!
notes: The Hebrew term occurs only here in the OT.
Here thorns may be a figure for hostility (Ezek 28:24; Mic 7:4).tn The Hebrew term is found elsewhere in the OT only in Ezek 28:24.
verses.commentary:
2:6 There is a series of commands from YHWH to Ezekiel.

- "neither fear," BDB 431, KB 432, Qal IMPERFECT, but used in
a JUSSIVE sense and repeated three times (cf. Jer. 1:8)

- "nor be dismayed," BDB 369, KB 365, Qal IMPERFECT, but used in
a JUSSIVE sense, cf. Josh. 10:25; Jer. 17:18

The reason Ezekiel is not to be afraid is YHWH's presence and promises (i.e. Deut. 31:8; Josh. 1:9;
1 Chr. 22:11-13; 28:20).

God uses several images to describe the reaction to Ezekiel's words by the rebellious house.

- thistles (BDB 709, KB 768, lit. "rebel," only here in the Hebrew Bible)

- thorns (BDB 699, KB 756, cf. Ezek. 28:24)

- scorpions (BDB 875, KB 875, cf. Deut. 8:15)

Numbers 1 and 2 are found only in Ezekiel. Israel did not want to hear from God. They wanted the covenant
blessings, but not the covenant requirements and consequences (cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28)!

Just a note to those of us who minister to God's people-they will not always appreciate or advocate
our ministry (i.e. Moses and Israel). We must remember who we serve and why! It is possible that the thorns, thistles,
and scorpions (possibly another thorny bush) refer to a hedge of God's protection around the prophet and his God-given
message.

verses.zh: 他们或听，或不听，你只管将我的话告诉他们；他们是极其悖逆的。
verses.en: You must speak my words to them whether they listen or not, for they are rebellious.
verses.commentary:
2:7 "whether they listen or not" This is repeated from Ezek. 2:5 and again in Ezek. 3:11. The same concept is
repeated in Ezek. 3:27. God will reveal Himself to His covenant people, even if they refuse to hear (cf. Isa. 6:9-13).
This is because

- He has an eternal redemptive purpose that involves Israel

- of His love for the Patriarchs

- of His character, bound to His promises

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

verses.zh: 人子啊，要听我对你所说的话，不要悖逆像那悖逆之家，你要开口吃我所赐给你的。」
verses.en: As for you, son of man, listen to what I am saying to you: Do not rebel like that rebellious house! Open your mouth and eat what I am giving you.”
verses.commentary:
2:8 "do not be rebellious like the rebellious house" Like Ezek. 2:6, Ezek. 2:8 has a series of commands from
YHWH to Ezekiel.

- "listen," BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal JUSSIVE

- "do not be rebellious," BDB 224, KB 243, Qal JUSSIVE

- "open your mouth," BDB 822, KB 953, Qal IMPERATIVE

- "eat," BDB 37, KB 46, Qal IMPERATIVE

Ezekiel's obedience constitutes his acceptance of YHWH's call to be His spokesperson. It is analogous
to

- the Seraph touching Isaiah's lips with a coal from the heavenly altar (i.e. Isa. 6:6-7; also note Jer. 1:9)

- Jeremiah's eating a scroll (cf. Jer. 15:16)

- John's vision in which an angel gives him a scroll to eat (cf. Rev. 10:8-11)

Obviously eating the scroll is imagery for receiving God's message and passing it on.

verses.zh: 我观看，见有一只手向我伸出来，手中有一书卷。
verses.en: Then I looked and realized a hand was stretched out to me, and in it was a written scroll.
verses.commentary:
2:9 "a hand was extended to me" The text is ambiguous as to whose hand was extended and from where. It could be
from the throne itself, but more likely, an attending angel, as in Isaiah 6.

▣ "a scroll" This would refer to a piece of papyrus rolled up (BDB 706). It symbolized the message of
God (cf. Isa. 29:11-12; 30:8; Jer. 25:13; 30:2; 36:2,4; Dan. 12:4).

Notice how the message of judgment on this scroll is described.

- lamentations (BDB 884)

- mourning (BDB 211)

- woe (BDB 223)

verses.zh: 他将书卷在我面前展开，内外都写着字，其上所写的有哀号、叹息、悲痛的话。
verses.en: He unrolled it before me, and it had writing on the front[NOTE:1] and back;[NOTE:2] written on it were laments, mourning, and woe.
notes: Written on the front and back. While it was common for papyrus scrolls to have writing on both sides, the same was not true for leather scrolls.
verses.commentary:
2:10 "It was written on the front and the back" It was highly unusual for either papyrus (i.e. hard to write
against the grain) or parchment (i.e. part of message can be worn off) to be written on both sides. This seems to be
imagery reflecting God's entire message of judgment (cf. Rev. 5:1). Once Jerusalem is destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar's army,
Ezekiel begins to proclaim restoration in YHWH's name (i.e. Ezekiel 36-37; 40-48).

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible.
Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing
is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.
